nameStory: The Question Mark butterfly gets its name from a distinctive silver marking on the underside of its hindwings that looks exactly like a question mark (?). This mark is formed by a curved line with a separate dot below it, creating nature's own punctuation mark that you can spot when the butterfly lands and folds its wings.
description: The Question Mark is a medium-sized butterfly with ragged, angular wing edges that make it look like a torn leaf. When its wings are open, you'll see orange-brown colors with dark spots and borders, but when closed, the mottled brown and gray underside provides perfect camouflage against tree bark and dead leaves. With a wingspan of about 2-3 inches, it's slightly larger than many of its comma butterfly relatives.

idTips.label: Silver question mark
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive silver question mark (curved line plus dot) on the brown underside of the hindwing - this is the only butterfly in New England with this exact marking

idTips.label: Ragged wing edges
idTips.description: Wing edges are deeply scalloped and irregular, creating a jagged silhouette that looks like torn or damaged leaves rather than smooth butterfly wings

idTips.label: Dead leaf camouflage
idTips.description: When wings are closed, the mottled brown, gray, and tan underside looks remarkably like a withered leaf, complete with darker lines resembling leaf veins

idTips.label: Orange upperside
idTips.description: Upper wing surfaces are bright orange-brown with black spots and dark borders - visible during flight or when basking with wings open

idTips.label: Size and flight
idTips.description: Noticeably larger than most other comma butterflies with a strong, erratic flight pattern that includes sudden stops and direction changes

habitat: Question Marks thrive in wooded areas with openings, including forest edges, city parks, suburban gardens, and anywhere trees meet open spaces. They prefer areas with elm, hackberry, and nettle plants where they can lay eggs, and are often found near tree sap, rotting fruit, or mud puddles. You'll spot them from ground level up to the forest canopy, as they're comfortable both in the understory and high in the trees.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter hibernation in April and May, often looking worn and faded from overwintering. Look for them basking on sunny tree trunks or feeding on early sap flows.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity from June through August with fresh, bright individuals from the summer brood. They're most active during warm afternoons, visiting flowers, rotting fruit, and dung.
seasonality.fall: Second brood adults appear in late summer and fall, with some individuals preparing for winter hibernation. Colors may appear more muted as they enter dormancy in October-November.
seasonality.winter: Adults hibernate in tree crevices, under loose bark, or in woodpiles. They're rarely seen but may emerge briefly during unusually warm winter days.

funFact: Question Mark butterflies are like flying wine connoisseurs - they have a strong preference for fermented fruit and tree sap, and males will actually get 'drunk' on fermenting apples, making them sluggish and easy to approach for photos!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Eastern Comma, but the Question Mark is noticeably larger and has that distinctive question mark symbol instead of the comma's simple curved line or 'C' shape on the wing underside. Memory trick: 'Question Mark = Question mark symbol, Eastern Comma = Comma symbol.'
compareHints: Among the comma butterflies, the Question Mark is the largest and the only one with the question mark punctuation mark on its underside. Eastern Commas have a simple curved silver line (like a comma), while other commas in the region have different silver markings or are much smaller. The Question Mark also tends to be more orange on top compared to the more brownish Eastern Comma.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's comma butterflies, Eastern Comma is distinguished by its bright silver comma mark (Green Comma has a greenish tint underneath, Gray Comma is more muted overall, and Hoary Comma has a more irregular silver mark).
Compared to the Eastern Comma, the Green Comma shows more greenish coloring on the underwing and tends to prefer more mountainous, forested areas rather than gardens and parks.
Among the comma butterflies, the Gray Comma is distinguished by its particularly prominent white comma mark and overall grayer underside coloration.
